questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I truly loved my exchange experience overall, but I faced significant challenges with the university’s administrative system. My teacher was without a doubt the best teacher I’ve ever had — incredibly dedicated and supportive. However, the institute itself was very disorganized. They issued us the wrong certificates, with incorrect nationalities and misspelled names. The administration had no understanding of Erasmus procedures, including the required number of teaching hours and the rules for attendance. At one point, they even threatened to reduce our hours due to misunderstandings about these rules. (<we consulted the teacher - (name removed) and fixed the misunderstanding) but this shouldnt be problems that the students should have to worry about

The teacher was not given any proper syllabus or plan from the institute, which caused a lack of clarity about what the University of Copenhagen required. Still, he managed to give us the best learning experience. this we consulted the teacher about (ulla) and also fixed the way through

The textbook we were given was also problematic. It was full of errors, and the texts were either too difficult or too easy — in both cases, completely mismatched with our actual level.

As for student life, it was also quite difficult. Especially for women, finding an apartment outside the university to avoid the 10 PM curfew was nearly impossible — if it hadn't been for Walid, a contact we got through our teacher Ulla, we wouldn’t have managed at all. Walid helped us with absolutely everything — things that were essential but that we had received no information about from the university. He spoke to the police to help us obtain our resident cards, arranged transportation, and made sure we understood how things worked both practically and academically. He also helped us understand the local culture and guided us into it — he even invited us to celebrate Eid with his family. When we had issues with our apartment, he came himself to help us. Without him, I honestly don’t know what I would have done. And yet, he isn’t even employed by the university. I strongly believe that the University of Copenhagen should consider the possibility of officially hiring him to support incoming students — without him, this experience would not have been possible.

Lastly, the location of the university is quite impractical unless you have a car and a driver’s license. Without that, I honestly wouldn't recommend going.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was not very easy to find the information I needed upon arrival. There was little planning in advance, and it felt more like we had to show up and figure things out ourselves. Luckily, everything worked out in the end because we received a lot of help from Walid.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn’t receive any real assistance from the institute, nor did I get the necessary information before or upon arrival. There was an initial meeting that explained what was supposed to happen at the university, but in reality, things turned out quite differently. Fortunately, our teacher helped us a lot in understanding how the university system worked and supported us in getting properly settled into it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: We didn’t receive any help with the process of getting our ID cards until 2–3 weeks after arrival, by which time Walid had already guided us through it. The card was needed much earlier, for example to get permission to drive a car in Oman and other essential things, so the lack of timely support was a real issue.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
uture students should be aware that living off-campus requires support in several areas. For example, as a woman, I found it difficult to communicate with our landlord because he started to develop an interest in me and sent me inappropriate messages. That’s why communication had to go through Walid, who understood the system and helped us manage the situation.

Additionally, there weren’t really any clear housing postings or  opportunities.

Some of my friends who lived on campus also found it challenging — the facilities were not very clean, and students with curfews had to be back by 10 PM, even in cases like school trips. One of my friends was even yelled at through voice messages for coming back late.

Living off-campus worked well for us and gave us more freedom, but you need the right kind of support — and that can be harder for women to access than for men.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be proactive and don’t hesitate to ask for what you need – things won’t always be clearly communicated.
2. You can learn a lot, especially linguistically and culturally, but make sure you know the academic requirements from UCPH and keep track of them.
3. If you’re well-prepared and stay flexible, everything will most likely work out well.
